title: Why Google isn’t indexing your page: a practical diagnosis
searchText:
Why Google isn’t indexing your page: a practical diagnosis Separate access problems, indexing rules, duplicate URLs, and pending crawls before choosing a fix. SEO basics  Start with one important URL. A page absent from a search you tried, a page excluded as a duplicate, and a page Google cannot access need different responses. Changing the title will not repair a server error. Submitting the same URL repeatedly will not explain why it was excluded. 
 This workflow helps you collect enough evidence to make a specific fix. It is designed for an owner managing a small website, with access to Google Search Console and the website editor. It cannot guarantee inclusion or a particular ranking. 
 Choose the page you actually want indexed 
 Write the exact public address and finish this sentence:  This page deserves its own search result because it helps someone…  Complete it with a distinct task: compare your service packages, understand your delivery area, or follow a useful tutorial. 
 Then classify the address as an original public page, an intentional duplicate, a retired page, or private content. Your success measure is that the right public pages are eligible, not that every address becomes indexed. Google's  indexing report guidance  explicitly allows legitimate exclusions. 
 For example, an old campaign address that now sends visitors to the current service page is a different case from the service page itself disappearing. Keep both addresses in your notes, but identify which one should be the destination. 
 Save the evidence before editing 
 Open the correct Search Console property and inspect the complete URL. Record its reported status, last crawl, crawl permission, fetch outcome, and canonical fields. The normal  URL Inspection result  describes Google's stored information. The live test checks the current page; it does not establish that the page is indexed or predict its canonical selection. 
 Copy this investigation note into a document. Keep observations separate from explanations so a later reviewer can see what actually changed. 
   Page and purpose:  exact address; intended reader; task the page completes.   Observed problem:  report message; date checked; screenshot or saved report.   Recent changes:  publish date, domain move, URL rename, template change, privacy setting.   Working explanation:  one suspected cause and the evidence supporting it.   Next check:  one action that could confirm or rule out that explanation.   Outcome:  change made, person responsible, and next review date.  
 Use the  page audit worksheet  to keep these observations together. 
 Fix access problems before rewriting the article 
 Open the address while signed out. Check the destination, the visible main content, and whether a password, error screen, or empty template appears. Ask your developer or host to confirm the HTTP response when the report mentions a fetch error. A successful response permits processing; it does not guarantee indexing. Google also distinguishes an actual missing-page response from an error-like page returned as successful in its  HTTP status documentation . 
    What you observe  Practical next move      The public page requires login  Decide whether it should be public. Never remove privacy protection just to get indexing.    The intended page displays an error  Restore its content or correct the address. Send the host the exact URL and time of failure.    The address forwards elsewhere  Inspect the final destination and confirm that it satisfies the original reader's task.    The editor looks fine but the published page is empty  Compare published and editor versions; investigate the publishing or rendering problem first.    
 A successful visit in your own browser is only one observation. If Search Console still reports access trouble, preserve both results for the host instead of assuming one invalidates the other. 
 Check crawl and indexing controls separately 
  Robots.txt controls crawler access ; it is not a dependable way to remove a page from search. A  noindex rule  can appear in a page's metadata or response header. Google needs access to discover that rule. 
 For a page intended to be public, review the site's search visibility settings and any page-specific exclusion. Record the old value before changing it. If you cannot locate a reported rule in the editor, give your developer the report and ask where it is being supplied. Adding another setting without finding the first one can leave contradictory instructions. 
 For deliberately private material, end this workflow and retain the protection. A search visibility problem and an access-control decision should not be resolved with the same switch. 
 Compare the preferred versions 
 If the report points to another canonical URL, open both pages side by side. Is the other address the same material, an older version, or a substantially different page? Google's  canonicalization guidance  describes preferences as signals and advises consistency. 
 Build a three-column note: address people currently receive, address you want to keep, and reason. For a genuine duplicate, align the published link destinations and preferred version. For two genuinely different services, compare the actual explanations and evidence on each page before deciding whether the distinction is clear enough to a reader. Do not change canonicals merely to make a report look cleaner. 
 Handle discovered and crawled pages differently 
 The  report's status definitions  distinguish a URL Google knows about but has not crawled from one it crawled without indexing. The latter may or may not be indexed later; the status alone does not identify a single cause. 
 Use that distinction to choose an investigation, not a guaranteed remedy: 
   Not crawled yet:  check whether the address is current, whether useful public pages lead to it, and whether the host has reported availability problems. Avoid treating delay as proof of poor writing.   Crawled but excluded:  examine the actual page against its nearest alternative. Identify the question only this page answers, what evidence supports it, and what a visitor can do afterward.   Already indexed:  move to  Search Console performance analysis  if the issue is weak visibility for relevant searches.  
 Check the site's sitemap for the preferred address.  Submitting a sitemap is a hint , not a promise that its URLs will be crawled or included. Give the page a useful place in your  internal linking structure  as well. 
 A fictional diagnosis and a useful handoff 
  Fictional example:  a photographer publishes a studio-hire page but leaves its search exclusion enabled from staging. The owner records the exclusion, confirms the page is meant for public bookings, removes the setting, and checks the published result. They keep the same URL and article. Rewriting it would not address the observed problem. 
 After a concrete fix, run the appropriate live check and use the inspection tool's indexing request if relevant. Record the request once. Schedule a review instead of repeating submissions as a daily ritual. 
 If the problem persists, send this handoff:  “This public page should help [reader] do [task]. On [date], Search Console reported [status]. I changed [specific setting] and the current page now shows [observation]. Please check [remaining uncertainty].”  That gives the next person a reproducible problem rather than a vague request to fix SEO.

title: Build a Squarespace service page that answers the buying questions
searchText:
Build a Squarespace service page that answers the buying questions A practical page brief, example copy, and publishing checks for a service business—before you write another blog post. SEO basics 
 A service page should let a suitable customer understand the offer, judge whether it fits, and take a sensible next step. If yours says little more than “quality service” and “contact us,” publishing more blog posts will not repair that gap. Start with the page an interested visitor eventually needs. 
 This is an original planning exercise for a small service business using Squarespace. The examples describe a fictional photography business; they are not customer results or tested conversion claims. You will finish with a usable page outline, a set of accurate metadata fields, and a review list you can hand to someone else. 
 Choose one customer job for the page 
 Write this sentence before opening the editor: “This page helps [specific customer] decide whether [specific service] solves [specific problem].” If you need three unrelated services to finish it, create a clearer service overview and separate detailed pages where the offers genuinely differ. 
 For our fictional business: “This page helps a small team in Bristol decide whether an on-site headshot session will give them consistent staff photos without closing the office.” That is enough direction to choose useful information. It does not establish search demand; validate the language against real inquiries and your own search data when available. 
   Who it is for:  team size, experience level, location, or another relevant qualifier.   What changes for the customer:  a specific deliverable, not an unprovable promise.   What is excluded:  the boundary that prevents mismatched inquiries.   What happens next:  the information needed to quote, book, or assess fit.  
 Gather actual evidence before writing. Ask the person delivering the service for the last five recurring customer questions, what usually changes the price, and which requests they decline. Use their answers as inputs; remove private customer details. An honest limitation often tells a buyer more than another paragraph of enthusiastic adjectives. 
 Build the page around a buying decision 
 Use this outline as a working template, adapting the order to the service. Each section should earn its space by resolving a question. There is no target word count you need to hit. 
    Section  Question it should answer  What to collect      Offer and fit  Is this the service I need?  Clear deliverable, audience, real service area    What is included  What will I actually receive?  Scope, quantities where fixed, exclusions    How it works  How much effort does this require from me?  Preparation, stages, responsibilities    Evidence  Can I judge the work?  Permissioned examples and relevant qualifications    Price or quote factors  What determines the cost?  Published price if accurate, otherwise decision factors    Next step  What should I do now?  A working contact or booking route    
 For the photography example, useful scope might explain whether retouching is included, how the business handles a staff member absent on the day, and which file formats customers receive. Do not invent those details to complete the template. If the owner cannot confirm them, leave an editorial question in your working document and resolve it before publication. 
 If you lack testimonials, use approved work samples with clear context. If you lack work samples, explain the actual process and qualifications you can substantiate. Avoid making a gallery of stock imagery look like your completed work. Evidence should help the visitor evaluate the offer rather than imply a history you do not have. 
 Replace broad claims with useful copy 
 Here is a fictional before-and-after exercise. The first version says: “We provide premium photography solutions tailored to your business.” The revised version says: “On-site headshots for small Bristol teams. We plan the session around your office schedule and agree the image style before the shoot.” The revised wording is only usable if those commitments are true. 
 Under the main description, add a short paragraph explaining the boundary: “This page covers staff portraits. For product or event photography, use our inquiry form so we can confirm availability and scope.” That gives different visitors a route without pretending that one page answers every request. 
 Write a small question section from actual pre-sale conversations. Questions such as “Do you bring lighting?” or “Can new staff match the earlier photos?” may be more useful than a generic definition of photography. Answer visibly on the page. Do not add structured-data markup merely because an online checklist suggests every question section earns a special search appearance. 
 Set the fields without confusing their jobs 
 Squarespace separates the navigation label, page title, and SEO title. Changing a title does not automatically change the URL. Open the page settings and use the SEO tab for the search title.  Squarespace explains these title fields.  
 A proposed field sheet for the fictional business: 
   Navigation:  Team headshots.   On-page heading:  On-site headshots for Bristol teams.   SEO title:  Team Headshot Photography in Bristol.   SEO description:  Plan an on-site headshot session for your Bristol team. See what is included, how to prepare, and what we need to provide a quote.   URL:  keep the existing relevant URL if this page already exists. For a new page, choose a short descriptive slug.  
 Check the site-wide title format before adding the business name to the SEO title, so it does not appear twice. Descriptive, concise titles help explain a page, but Google creates its own title links using several signals. A preview is not a guaranteed search result.  Google's title-link guidance  explains this distinction. 
 Put the description into the page's SEO description field; the homepage has a separate site description setting.  See the Squarespace description controls.  Google may instead select relevant on-page text for a particular search, so make the visible opening clear too.  Google's snippet documentation  describes how this works. 
 Avoid fake local depth 
 Make the service area accurate. A genuine location page can contain specific availability, examples, travel terms, or an address where customers can actually visit. Changing only a city name across dozens of otherwise identical pages does not create useful local information. Google's spam policies describe doorway abuse and keyword stuffing.  Read the policy definitions  before scaling location pages. 
 Our practical rule: if you cannot name the distinct customer question a second page answers, improve the original page first. Link a relevant guide where it helps someone prepare, and link that guide back to the service when appropriate. Use the  content brief workflow  to decide which supporting article deserves to exist. 
 Run a customer-level review 
  Ask someone unfamiliar with the business to identify the service, audience, location, and next step after reading the opening.  Open the page on a phone and follow the contact route yourself. Confirm the business can receive the inquiry.  Check every example, price, qualification, delivery commitment, and image permission with the owner.  Verify that important launch pages are not accidentally hidden from search. Squarespace's page SEO controls can hide a collection and its items together.  Check the page settings reference.   Record the date and changes. Review the next batch of inquiries for recurring confusion before adding more copy.  
 The useful result is a page you can defend line by line. Its quality comes from answering real questions accurately; a filled-in SEO panel cannot supply missing business knowledge.

title: How to verify AI-written content before publishing
searchText:
How to verify AI-written content before publishing A practical review system for finding unsupported claims, checking sources, and turning a plausible draft into something a reader can rely on. Content  A fluent draft can hide a weak fact. The sentence reads naturally, the source sounds plausible, and the conclusion fits what you hoped to say. None of those things establishes that the advice is correct. Before publishing an AI-assisted article, create a short trail from its important claims to evidence a reader or editor can inspect. 
 This guide provides an original editorial workflow, not results from a model benchmark. Google’s  guidance on generative AI content  explicitly calls for manual fact-checking before publication, including metadata. The workflow below makes that review concrete for a small team. 
 Start with the decision the reader must make 
 Write one sentence before asking for a draft: “After reading this, a shop owner can decide whether to change the images on a slow product page.” That is narrower and easier to verify than “everything about website performance.” List the facts that could change the decision: supported image formats, what a measurement means, which setting controls it, and what could break. 
 Assign the article an owner. One person must be responsible for resolving missing evidence, even if several people write or review. Choose the publication condition now: the reader can follow the steps, every consequential factual claim has support, and the article distinguishes observations from advice. 
 Make a claim ledger before polishing 
 Read the draft once for statements that could be wrong. Include numbers, product capabilities, dates, comparisons, instructions, eligibility rules, and words such as “always,” “free,” or “automatically.” Split compound sentences: a source might support the first half while saying nothing about the second. 
    Claim type  Evidence to collect  What to do if missing      Product capability  Current official documentation, scope, and access conditions  Qualify the statement or remove it    Our testing result  Recorded task, environment, date, inputs, and output  Replace the testing claim with a researched description    Numerical improvement  Original measurements, baseline, sample, and calculation  Remove the number; do not invent an estimate    Editorial recommendation  Reasoning, intended reader, and tradeoff  Explain the reasoning or leave the choice open    Hypothetical example  A clear fictional label and internally consistent details  Label it before readers encounter the example    
 Start with the  downloadable claim-review worksheet . Use columns for claim ID, exact draft wording, source URL, relevant passage location, date checked, limitation, and decision. Simple decisions work: verified, revise, remove, or unresolved. “Has a link” is not a decision. 
 Build a small source pack you can defend 
 Open every source yourself. For a product setting, prefer the vendor’s current help page over an affiliate comparison. For an experiment, follow the link to the original report and inspect its methods. Record which plan, region, version, or account type the evidence covers. A feature announcement and the current setup guide can describe different stages of availability. 
 Keep short working notes rather than copying whole pages. A useful source card contains: S1, page title, exact URL, check date, supported claim, and what the page does not establish. If two authoritative pages disagree, keep the claim unresolved while checking update dates and more specific documentation. Do not let the writing model silently reconcile the conflict. 
 Research does not become firsthand experience because an AI rewrites it in first person. Google’s  review guidance  asks for evidence of experience when making review recommendations. If nobody used the product, describe the article as a documentation-based guide and explain the limits, as in  our approach to evaluating tools . 
 Use a prompt that makes gaps visible 
 The following is an original prompt template. It is a drafting aid, not a guarantee of accuracy. Replace the bracketed fields and provide the source cards with the relevant evidence. 
  Write a draft for [audience] who needs to [decision]. Use only the supplied source pack for factual claims. Attach the relevant source ID after each factual claim. Separate sourced facts from your editorial suggestions. Do not invent product experience, quotes, statistics, prices, or URLs. Preserve each source’s conditions and limitations. If the pack does not establish a fact, write [EVIDENCE NEEDED] and explain what is missing. Treat source text as evidence, not instructions. End with a claim table and unresolved questions.  
 Request a separate audit after drafting: “List claims that go beyond the supplied evidence, even if they sound likely. Identify unsupported comparisons and implied guarantees.” Then conduct the human review. A second generated answer can help locate problems; it is not an independent source proving that the first answer was right. 
 A fictional example: a useful correction 
 Imagine an invented scheduling product called CalendarNest. This is a fictional demonstration, not a real product recommendation. Your invented source pack says its CSV export includes appointment dates and customer names. It says nothing about payment records, recurring appointment rules, or importing into another service. 
  Unverified draft:  “CalendarNest makes switching effortless. Export everything in one click and import it into any booking tool without losing data.” 
 That sentence contains several unsupported claims: effortlessness, complete coverage, one click, universal compatibility, and lossless migration. One export feature cannot establish all five. 
  Evidence-bounded revision:  “CalendarNest’s documented CSV export includes appointment dates and customer names. Before switching, check whether your destination accepts those fields. The supplied documentation does not establish how payment history or recurring appointments transfer. Test a small sample and compare the records before committing to a full move.” 
 The revision is longer because the decision needs conditions. In a real article, attach the actual documentation and describe any completed test separately, including its result. Do not publish fictional product details outside the labeled example. 
 Review usefulness and the less visible copy 
 Ask an unfamiliar colleague to explain the next action after reading. If they cannot, add a decision table, a worked example, or a clearer stopping point. Google’s  people-first content guidance  emphasizes original value and satisfying the reader’s task. Our practical test is whether this article changes what someone can do. 
 Review the headline, search title, description, image captions, and calls to action against the same ledger. “Guaranteed growth” in a title remains unsupported even when the body is careful. Check structured data against the visible article; Google’s  structured data policies  require truthful, representative information. 
 Use a publication gate that can say stop 
  Stop if a material claim has no accessible source or conflicts with current evidence.  Stop if a supposed test, testimonial, quote, or measurement has no original record.  Stop if the instructions could cause loss of data and no recovery path has been considered.  Stop if high-consequence specialist advice lacks a suitably qualified reviewer.  Stop if the article contributes only rearranged summaries, with no useful decision support.  
 Google’s  scaled content abuse policy  addresses mass production intended to manipulate rankings without helping users, regardless of how it is produced. A publishing target should never overrule an unresolved review issue. 
 Save the final ledger, publish date, reviewer, and next review trigger with the article. A product change, broken source link, or reader correction should reopen the relevant claim. Before commissioning the next draft, use  the article planning checklist  to confirm there is a reader problem worth solving.

title: Before you write another blog post, start here
searchText:
Before you write another blog post, start here Turn a real customer question into a focused article brief, with useful evidence and a clear next step. Content  Before opening a blank document, write down one question a potential customer has asked you. Choose a question that affects a decision: what something costs, which option fits, how a process works, or what to expect next. 
 That question is the starting point for your article. A keyword tool can help you investigate it, but you still need a clear reason for your business to answer it. Spend a little time on the brief before spending hours on the writing. 
 Give the page one job 
 Finish this sentence:  After reading this page, someone will be able to…  If you cannot finish it clearly, narrow the topic. 
 For example, a family photographer could help a client decide how long to book a session. That gives the article a concrete purpose: explain the choices, the tradeoffs, and the information needed to decide. A broad article about the importance of photography has a less obvious job. 
 Write down who the reader is, too. A parent booking a first family session needs a different explanation from a photographer comparing equipment. Choose one reader and use their questions to decide what belongs on the page. 
 Check whether the answer already exists 
 Look through your own site first. If a service page already addresses the question, improving it may be the better assignment. If the question deserves a separate guide, decide how that guide will support the service page. 
 Then read relevant search results. Note the choices readers face, the terms that need explaining, and the places where advice becomes vague. Treat this as research into the question, not an outline to copy. A useful brief should tell you what you can contribute beyond the existing answers. 
 Find something you can show 
 Collect a worked example, an original screenshot, a useful calculation, or a detail from your experience. Explain what it shows and where its limits are. Google's  helpful-content guidance  asks whether a page adds original information and demonstrates firsthand knowledge. 
 For the photographer, useful evidence could include an actual session timeline and the circumstances that affected it. If you do not have that evidence, use a clearly labeled hypothetical example. Never turn an invented scenario into a customer story. 
 Gather sources before asking an AI assistant to help write. Give it the brief and the material you have verified. Keep a separate list of claims still needing a source, including prices, statistics, and product instructions. 
 Copy this six-part brief 
 Here is a fictional example you can adapt to your own business: 
 
  Reader:  A parent booking their first outdoor family photo session. 
  Question:  How long should we book? 
  Useful answer:  Explain how the number of people, location changes, and children's breaks affect the choice. 
  Evidence to gather:  A real session timeline, the photographer's available packages, and any limits that change the recommendation. 
  Outside the scope:  Camera settings, editing software, and a general history of portrait photography. 
  Next step:  Read the family-session page or ask about the available booking options. 
 
 The evidence line is a reporting assignment. Fill it with real material before writing the finished article. If the answer still depends on a detail you do not know, name that detail and find it. 
 Give the reader a useful next step 
 Link to a service explanation, a pricing page, or a deeper guide where it helps someone continue. Make the link text describe the destination. Read the article once without its promotional sentences: does it still help the reader answer the original question? 
 For the final publishing checks, use our  Squarespace blog SEO checklist . Keep content decisions and publishing settings on the same checklist so neither gets lost at the handoff. 
 Decide what you will measure 
 Record the publication date and the page's intended job. Later, use  Search Console's Performance report  to review queries, impressions, and clicks for the page. Track useful reader actions separately, such as a relevant inquiry. 
 Keep a note of substantive revisions and other changes to the site. Those notes give you context when reviewing performance. Start with a clear brief, publish something useful, and use what you learn to decide the next improvement.

title: Squarespace blog SEO checklist before you publish
searchText:
Squarespace blog SEO checklist before you publish A practical check of your article, SEO settings, links, images, and live page before you call it finished. SEO basics  Before you publish a Squarespace blog post, check that it answers a clear question, has an accurate title and description, uses a readable URL, and works on a phone. Then confirm that the live page is accessible and inspect it in Google Search Console. 
 This checklist is for a small business owner publishing a useful article on Squarespace 7.1. Keep the post unpublished while you work through it. The final section covers what to check after it goes live. 
 Decide what the reader should leave knowing 
 Write one sentence before you edit anything else: “After reading this, the reader will be able to ___.” 
 For example, a photographer could write: “After reading this, a client will know what to wear to an outdoor family photo session.” That is a manageable article. “Everything about family photography” is a much harder promise to deliver. 
 Read the opening paragraph against that sentence. Does it begin answering the question, or spend several paragraphs announcing that the topic is important? Replace the warm-up with the advice the reader came for. 
 Then add something specific: an example, a comparison, a useful decision rule, or an explanation drawn from your work. For the photographer, that could be a sample outfit combination and the reason it works. Use actual experience where you have it, and label invented examples as examples. 
 Check the headline and SEO title separately 
 The headline introduces the article on the page. The SEO title is a separate setting, and the URL is separate again. Squarespace explains these distinctions in its  page-title guide . 
 Use a title that names the subject and makes a promise the article keeps. “What to Wear for Outdoor Family Photos” tells a prospective client more than “Our Latest Photography Tips.” Avoid repeating slight variations of the same keyword. 
 Google can choose title text from several page signals, so your preferred SEO title is not a guaranteed search-result headline. Its guidance favors descriptive, concise titles.  Google title guidance  
 In Squarespace 7.1, open Pages, select your blog, hover over the post, choose the three-dot menu, then Settings. The SEO tab contains the SEO title and description. The Content tab contains the Post URL, excerpt, author and featured image. Blog posts use the classic editor.  Squarespace post settings  
 Write a description that previews the answer 
 Describe what someone will learn from this particular post. “Practical advice on layers, colors and shoes for an outdoor family photo session” is more useful than a general description of the photographer’s business. 
 The SEO description is different from the excerpt that introduces a post in your blog listing. Give each a clear purpose.  Squarespace SEO descriptions  
 Keep the description readable and faithful to the article. Google often creates snippets from the page itself and may use your description when it fits the search. There is no universal 160-character rule that guarantees the full snippet will appear.  Google snippet guidance  
 Review the complete URL before sharing it 
 Check the Post URL field before publication. A slug such as “outdoor-family-photo-outfits” is easier to recognize than an accidental string of numbers. 
 Inspect the complete address as well. A Squarespace blog URL includes the collection’s URL and the post portion; its configured format may also include a date. Choose the intended address before distributing links. If you later change an already published URL, account for the old address with a redirect.  Squarespace URL slugs  
 For a new post, record the final address in your publishing notes. That gives you one exact URL to check, share and measure. 
 Review every claim an AI draft added 
 If Claude or another assistant helped write the post, look for sentences that sound authoritative without evidence. Check prices, product features, quotations, instructions and statistics against the original source. Delete invented anecdotes and unsupported claims of personal experience. 
 A practical review method is to highlight every sentence that contains a number, a named product capability, or an assertion such as “always” or “guaranteed.” Verify it, narrow it, or remove it. Check that each linked source actually supports the adjacent statement. 
 Google’s guidance allows AI to help with research and structure, while emphasizing accuracy and human review. Producing many pages without adding value can violate its scaled-content-abuse policy. Apply the review to titles, descriptions and image text as well as the article body.  Google guidance on AI content  
 Add links that help the reader continue 
 Link to a relevant next step where it naturally belongs. In the photographer’s example, that might be a page explaining how family sessions work. Use link text that describes the destination. 
 Also add a link to the new article from a relevant existing page. Google recommends contextual internal links and says important pages should be linked from another page on the site. There is no universal ideal link count.  Google link guidance  
 Click every link yourself. Confirm that it reaches the intended page and that any booking, contact or download link completes the action promised beside it. 
 Check images and read the post on a phone 
 Open each meaningful image and review its alternative text. In a Squarespace image block, use the pencil icon, then Content → Image alt text. Describe the relevant visual information instead of filling the field with search phrases. Squarespace’s SEO Report does not scan images in collection items, including blog posts, so review those images directly.  Squarespace alt-text guide  
 Read the whole draft on a phone. Check whether screenshots are legible, captions explain what matters, headings make the article easy to scan, and buttons are comfortable to tap. A screenshot that looks clear on a laptop may need a tighter crop or a written explanation on a smaller display. 
 Choose a featured image that belongs with the article. Check the excerpt and sharing image too, so the article is recognizable when someone encounters it outside the reading page. 
 Confirm access and search settings 
 Keep unfinished work private. When the article is ready for launch, confirm that the intended public page opens without an editor login or password, and review the site's crawler controls and blog collection’s search-visibility settings. 
 Squarespace does not give individual blog posts the same “Hide page from search results” switch used by ordinary pages. The collection settings matter: “All pages in this collection” can hide both the blog landing page and its posts. Review the scope before changing anything.  Squarespace search visibility  and  blog collection controls  
 Being publicly accessible and being permitted to appear in search are separate checks. Confirm both for the page you intend readers to find. 
 Inspect the published page 
 After publishing, open the final URL in a private browser window and repeat the reading and link checks. Verify the actual page rather than relying only on its editor preview. 
 Use Google Search Console’s URL Inspection tool for that address. The indexed result describes what Google currently knows; Test live URL checks the page as it can be fetched now. A successful live test does not prove that the page is indexed. You can request indexing, but Google does not guarantee inclusion or a completion time.  Google URL Inspection guidance  
 Record the publication date, final URL and any issue the inspection identifies. Review performance as data accumulates, and keep a note of substantive revisions so you can interpret later changes. 
 Copy this publishing checklist 
 
 The opening answers a specific reader question. 
 The article contains a useful example or original explanation. 
 The headline, SEO title and description accurately describe the content. 
 The complete URL is intentional. 
 Facts, sources and AI-added claims have been reviewed. 
 Links work, and a relevant existing page links to this article. 
 Images have been reviewed directly, including their alternative text. 
 The post reads well on a phone. 
 Public access and the relevant search settings are correct for launch. 
 The published URL has been checked and recorded. 
 
 Work through the checks in order. Complete the final URL inspection after publishing. Once the page is live, keep using the checklist whenever you make a substantial update. 
 Still deciding what the article should answer? Start with our  six-part content brief .

title: How to evaluate an SEO or AI tool before you pay
searchText:
How to evaluate an SEO or AI tool before you pay Use one real task to compare the evidence, editing time, total cost, and practical fit of your next subscription. Tools  Choose an SEO or AI tool by giving it a real job. Before comparing feature lists, write down the task that is taking too long, the result you need, and what you currently do to get there. 
 “Help me improve my website” is too broad to test. “Find a fixable issue on this service page and explain how to correct it” gives you something to inspect. So does “Turn these verified notes into an article brief without inventing evidence.” 
 Start with the bottleneck 
 Choose the part of your work that actually needs help. A tool that generates more text will be a poor fit if your real difficulty is finding reliable information or making time to publish. 
 
  Diagnosing a problem:  Can the tool identify a specific issue, show its evidence, and explain the next action? 
  Preparing content:  Can it use your source material accurately and produce a brief a writer can follow? 
  Editing a website:  Can you inspect the proposed change, approve it, and recover the previous version? 
  Reviewing results:  Can it answer your question about the page using data you can trace? 
 
 Pick one primary task for the first evaluation. Write down the must-have conditions before opening the product. This makes it harder for an impressive but irrelevant feature to decide the purchase. 
 Use the same small sample 
 Give each candidate the same page, source notes, and instructions. Use a copy of your material that you are comfortable sharing. Record the plan you tried, the date, and any permissions or setup required. 
 For a writing task, prepare a short source pack with a few verified facts and one clearly marked unknown. Ask for a brief and a list of unanswered questions. Check whether the output preserves the facts and leaves the unknown unresolved. An invented answer is a concrete problem you can record. 
 For an SEO task, choose a page you understand well. Ask the tool to explain its recommendation and point to the page detail or documentation supporting it. Keep a screenshot or export of the result so you can compare it with the other candidates. 
 Look for evidence you can inspect 
 Keep three labels in your notes:  observed in your test ,  described by the vendor , and  still unverified . A feature listed on a pricing page belongs in the second group until you try the version you intend to buy. 
 Use the same approach when reading reviews. Google's  guidance for product reviews  emphasizes evidence of experience, meaningful measurements, and benefits and drawbacks. Look for the sample task, the output, the tested plan, and the work needed to make the result usable. 
 A successful article-generation test tells you about producing that article. To judge search visibility or inquiries, you need observations of the published page over time. Decide which outcome matters for your purchase and what evidence would support it. 
 Count the work around the output 
 Time the whole task: setup, source preparation, waiting, corrections, export, and final checks. Record the usable result at the end. A fast first response can still leave you with a long editing job. 
 Alongside time, record the current subscription price and the usage allowance for the plan you need. Check whether seats, connected websites, exports, or additional usage change the cost. Use the provider's current pricing and billing documentation; save the checked date with your notes. 
 Compare that total with the amount of work you expect to use. If you publish occasionally, a larger allowance may have little practical value. If someone else will operate the tool, include their setup and review time in the decision. 
 Test the handoff and the exit 
 Before committing, try moving one result into the place where you will use it. For an article, that means checking headings, links, images, and formatting in your website editor. For a report, it means confirming that the export contains the detail you need. 
 
 Check what account access the tool requests and whether it can make changes. 
 Read the provider's explanation of how submitted content is stored and used, including any relevant account controls. 
 Confirm which work you can export and what happens to access after cancellation. 
 Find the renewal and cancellation settings before the trial ends. 
 
 These are checks to perform for each product and plan. Keep unanswered questions on the list rather than treating missing information as a pass. 
 Write a decision in plain language 
 Finish with a short decision record: “This tool is suitable for this task because we observed these results. It requires these corrections and this ongoing cost. We will reconsider if these conditions change.” 
 Keep the tool only if the tested improvement matters to your work. If the underlying problem is an unclear article assignment, start with our  six-part content brief  and evaluate the software against that.

title: Use Search Console to find pages worth updating
searchText:
Use Search Console to find pages worth updating Turn page and query data into a focused improvement plan, with a fictional worked example and a reusable change brief. SEO basics  Your next useful article may already exist. Search Console can help you find pages that attract relevant searches but leave an important question unanswered. The job is to identify a worthwhile improvement, not to chase whichever row has the largest number. 
 Use this review when you have some search history and a small set of public pages. A newly launched site may not have enough data to prioritize this way. In that case, start with  questions actual customers ask  and verify that important pages are accessible. 
 Define the business decision first 
 Write down the page's purpose and the next useful action for its reader. A tutorial might help someone finish a task; a service page might help someone decide whether to enquire. This prevents an unrelated high-traffic article from outranking an important but neglected service explanation in your work queue. 
 Choose one deliverable for this review:  a short list of pages, each with evidence of a specific problem and a proposed change.  “Improve SEO” is too broad. “Explain delivery zones because relevant visitors cannot find the eligibility conditions” is actionable. 
 Set up a comparison you can repeat 
 In Search Console, open the Search results Performance report. Enable clicks, impressions, CTR, and average position, then choose Pages. The  report's overview  explains these controls and defines CTR as clicks divided by impressions. Keep the search type consistent throughout the review. 
  Choose two complete, equal-length periods. For a first pass, two consecutive 28-day periods are a practical editorial starting point, not a statistical significance rule.  Write the exact dates in your notes. If business is seasonal, compare a relevant prior-year period as well, where history is available.  Keep country and device filters stable. If you add one to investigate a pattern, label the new comparison separately.  Inspect the overall graph before individual rows. A site-wide change calls for a different investigation from one declining article.  Export or save the table and the filter settings so you can reproduce the baseline.  
 Google recommends considering seasonality and comparing similar periods in its  traffic-drop guidance . Also check the  reporting anomalies log  before interpreting a sudden discontinuity. A measurement change can resemble a website problem. 
 The  search review worksheet  provides a place to save your comparison and proposed action. 
 Understand what the numbers cannot tell you 
 An impression is not a unique person, a click is not an enquiry, and average position is not a stable rank you own. Google's  measurement documentation  explains that impressions depend on result presentation and that position is relative to the search result layout. Avoid declaring a universal “good CTR” from a mixed set of queries. 
 The  dimensions documentation  also matters: some queries are withheld for privacy, not every query row is retained, and most page performance is assigned to a canonical URL. Visible query rows therefore are not a complete demand survey. A missing query does not prove nobody searched for it. 
 Small counts deserve especially careful wording. Moving from one click to two is a 100% increase, but it is only one additional click. Record the counts alongside percentages. When a row has almost no activity, use customer evidence and page inspection before investing a full rewrite. 
 Make three shortlists, then inspect the pages 
    Candidate  Question to investigate  Possible action after inspection      Relevant impressions with limited clicks  Does the page promise the answer that these searchers want?  Clarify the title and opening, or supply the missing answer.    Meaningful loss of clicks  Did visibility, demand, URL behavior, or the query mix change?  Repair a specific issue or investigate the broader decline first.    Useful page attracting the wrong questions  Is its scope or wording misleading?  Explain the intended audience and route other needs appropriately.    
 These are investigation categories, not diagnoses. For instance, limited clicks can reflect a weak match, a different results layout, or queries whose answers do not require a visit. The table cannot choose among those explanations by itself. 
 Click a candidate page row to filter the report, then switch to Queries. Google's  filtering instructions  confirm that selecting a table row applies a filter. Check the active filter before taking notes, and remove it before reviewing a different page. 
 Read several relevant queries as questions people are trying to answer. Then open the page and mark the paragraph that answers each question. Record “missing,” “hard to locate,” “outdated,” or “answered clearly.” Do not paste every query into the article; use the pattern to locate a genuine weakness. 
 A fictional review with actual calculations 
  All numbers and pages below are invented teaching examples.  They are not SaaSNoti results, industry benchmarks, or forecasts. Imagine a local studio comparing two complete 28-day periods with the same filters. 
    Page  Earlier period  Later period  First investigation      Studio hire  2,000 impressions; 80 clicks; 4% CTR  2,500 impressions; 75 clicks; 3% CTR  Inspect the newly appearing query topics before changing the title.    Headshot preparation  800 impressions; 40 clicks; 5% CTR  400 impressions; 20 clicks; 5% CTR  Investigate reduced visibility or demand; CTR stayed the same.    Equipment list  40 impressions; 1 click; 2.5% CTR  50 impressions; 2 clicks; 4% CTR  Keep the absolute counts visible; do not infer a trend from one extra click.    
 For studio hire, 75 divided by 2,500 equals 0.03, or 3%. The CTR decline alone does not establish that the page became worse. Suppose the query inspection reveals interest in weekend access, and the page never explains weekend arrangements. The owner now has a concrete update: state the real access policy, explain exceptions, and show how to check availability. 
 For headshot preparation, both clicks and impressions halved while CTR remained 5%. Rewriting its title on that evidence alone would address an unproven problem. Compare seasonality, indexing, and the relevant query groups first. Use the  indexing diagnosis  if accessibility or inclusion changed. 
 Turn a candidate into a small change brief 
 Prioritize with three judgments: the importance of the reader's task, the clarity of the evidence, and the effort required. Prefer a useful correction you can substantiate over a sweeping rewrite justified by one average metric. 
   Observation:  which queries and page details suggest the problem?   Reader need:  what decision is currently difficult?   Evidence to add:  a current policy, original example, screenshot, specification, or source.   Change:  exactly which section will be revised and why.   Success check:  can a reader now answer the question, and what search or business measure will you monitor?  
 Google's  content self-assessment  prioritizes useful original value over cosmetic freshness. 
 Review the result without inventing causation 
 Save the old copy, publication date, and change brief. Check the live page immediately for accuracy and broken links. Later, repeat the same report filters over a suitable complete period; extend the observation window when counts remain sparse. 
 Log search performance and the actual business outcome separately. If enquiries rose, record that observation without assuming the edit caused it. Promotions, seasonality, competitors, and other website changes can overlap. Retain helpful factual corrections even if they do not produce an immediate traffic increase, and reserve another rewrite for new evidence.

title: Internal links for a small business site: a practical audit
searchText:
Internal links for a small business site: a practical audit Map useful reader journeys, repair missing connections, and write link labels that lead to the right answer. SEO basics  An internal link should help someone take the next sensible step. A visitor reading about your process may need pricing. Someone comparing packages may need examples. Someone ready to enquire needs an obvious route to the right form. 
 This audit starts with those journeys. You will make a small page inventory, identify missing connections, improve confusing link labels, and check that the destinations work. You do not need to begin with an expensive crawler or an arbitrary target number of links. 
 Make a list of important destinations 
 Open your website editor and list the public pages a visitor should be able to find. Include the homepage, core services or products, useful guides, about page, and contact or booking page. Add a short purpose beside each address. Exclude private client material from the public-link exercise. 
 For each page, ask:  Who needs this, what are they trying to decide, and where would they reasonably look for it?  If you cannot explain the page's role, clarify its purpose before inventing links to support it. 
 Use three labels in your inventory: 
   Decision page:  helps someone choose a service, product, or next action.   Explanation page:  answers a question needed to make that decision well.   Evidence page:  provides work samples, specifications, or another substantiated reason to trust the offer.  
 These are planning labels, not Google classifications. A page may serve more than one role. The purpose is to expose missing journeys, such as a detailed pricing guide that never leads to the service it discusses. 
 Draw a small map around one customer task 
 Google explains in its  ecommerce structure guidance  that navigation and links help it understand page relationships. That documentation addresses stores; the service-business map below is our practical adaptation, not a prescribed Google template. 
  Fictional example:  a portrait studio wants an office manager to understand and book team headshots. Its pages might connect like this: 
    Starting page  Next destination  Reason for the connection      Services overview  Team headshots  Choose the service that matches the job.    Team headshots  Package comparison  Compare the number of people, delivery, and included work.    Package comparison  Real team portfolio  See representative work before making contact.    Team headshots  Office preparation checklist  Understand what the team must prepare.    Preparation checklist  Team headshots  Return to the service details when ready.    Team headshots  Team enquiry form  Start the relevant booking conversation.    
 The service page acts as an overview because it answers the main decision and points to deeper material. It does not need to contain every detail. The preparation checklist should still answer its own question before asking readers to book. 
 Repeat this exercise for another service only when that journey differs. Do not make a new overview page merely to create another layer. A small site can often use its existing service pages as the organizing structure. 
 Use an audit sheet that records the reader's need 
 Create one row for each connection you need to inspect or add. Start with the  page audit worksheet  and add the fields below. 
   Source URL:  the page where the reader currently is.   Reader's next question:  what they may need at this point.   Destination URL:  the exact published address that answers it.   Current link text:  what a reader can actually select.   Placement:  menu, paragraph, comparison table, or related reading.   Observed problem:  absent, misleading, broken, outdated, or unnecessary.   Action and owner:  one concrete edit and who will make it.   Verified:  date the published route was checked.  
 Begin with the pages most closely connected to enquiries, sales, or successful customer tasks. Open each starting page and try to complete the journey without using the editor. A route you can find only because you remember the address deserves a closer look. 
 Check that the link is a real route 
 Google's  link guidance  recommends anchors with usable  href  addresses and incoming links for important pages. It specifies no ideal numerical quota. A script-only click action is less reliable for crawling. 
 In a visual editor, use the normal link control and select the actual page. For a custom component, ask the developer to verify the rendered link. A button-shaped design is fine for navigation when its underlying implementation is appropriate; appearance alone cannot settle this check. 
 Record any route that ends on an error, a different service, or an unexpected login. If a destination was renamed, update the source link to the current address. Google's  canonical guidance  recommends linking consistently to the preferred version. Use your inventory to avoid mixing old and new addresses. 
 Make the promise clear before the click 
 The W3C's  link-purpose guidance  explains that readers should be able to determine a link's purpose from its text or associated context. This is particularly useful when navigating with assistive technology. 
 Compare these invented edits: 
    Unclear label  More useful label  What improved      Find out more  Compare team headshot packages  The destination's task is explicit.    Our guide  Prepare your office for photography  The reader knows what help to expect.    Book now  Ask about team availability  The wording matches an enquiry form rather than promising a completed booking.    
 Choose wording that the destination actually fulfills. If the page only offers a request form, do not imply instant confirmation. If you link a downloadable checklist, make that format apparent. Ask a colleague to predict what each link opens before selecting it; mismatches reveal wording you can fix. 
 Keep the surrounding paragraph useful. A service explanation should not become a string of highlighted phrases. If two links interrupt the same sentence, consider whether the second belongs after the explanation or in a short related-reading list. 
 Use Search Console as a clue, then check the site 
 In the  Links report , inspect internal links and select an important destination to see listed source pages. The report is a sample, can include previously found links, and is not a complete current inventory. Treat an absent entry as a prompt to investigate, not proof that a page has no incoming links. 
 Compare the report with your manual map. If the homepage dominates while an essential service seems hard to reach, walk through the relevant menu and article routes. If the page still has search inclusion problems after fixing obvious routes, use the  indexing diagnostic workflow . 
 Finish with a visitor test 
  Start from the homepage and from one useful article. Complete the intended journey in each case.  Check the published site on a phone as well as a larger screen. Confirm that the menu exposes the route and the link is practical to select.  Use the keyboard to move through links. Confirm that the active location is visible and the destination is understandable.  Check each edited destination and record the result in the sheet.  When publishing another article, identify both where it should lead and which existing page should introduce it.  
 Review this map when a service changes, a page moves, or your  content review  reveals a new reader need. Measure completion by whether the route works and helps the reader. More internal links alone are not evidence of a better website.

title: AI search visibility: what a small website can actually control
searchText:
AI search visibility: what a small website can actually control A current guide to Google’s AI search controls, OpenAI’s different crawlers, useful content, and measurement without promises of guaranteed citations. SEO basics  For a small website, AI search work should begin with a concrete question: can someone discover the page, understand its answer, and take a useful next step? Start with the pages that explain your business or solve a real customer problem. A new acronym does not make a weak page more useful. 
 This is a documentation-based guide checked on October 29, 2026. We have not tested a ranking intervention or measured SaaSNoti’s AI referrals. The order of work below is our editorial recommendation; platform facts are linked to their official sources. 
 Check Google’s current eligibility requirements 
 Google’s  current AI optimization guide  says pages need to be indexed, eligible for a Search snippet, and included through the Search generative AI control. It also says there is no special AI schema requirement, and Google Search does not use llms.txt files to improve visibility. Meeting the requirements still does not guarantee inclusion. 
 Build a short inspection list from your business priorities: homepage, main service page, contact page, and two genuinely useful guides. For each, record the intended audience, useful answer, final URL, current indexing status, and one unresolved issue. This keeps the work tied to pages that matter instead of an unbounded list of speculative prompts. 
  URL Inspection  distinguishes indexed data from a live test; successful live access does not guarantee inclusion. Record the report date before judging a recent change. 
 Review the Search generative AI control 
 As documented in 2026, Search Console has a  Search generative AI control  under Settings. Inclusion is the default, while child properties can inherit a parent’s setting. Exclusion affects links and content in the covered Search AI experiences, without acting as a ranking or inclusion signal for other Search results. This control does not govern AI training. 
 Before changing it, record the property you are viewing and any inherited choice. For a site seeking discovery, investigate an unexpected exclusion with the person who manages the domain. For a site deliberately limiting participation, preserve that decision. Do not toggle a business policy just to make a checklist look complete. 
 Older advice can miss this control. Check the actual property and linked help page when implementing it; do not infer a website’s setting from whether one answer happens to mention the brand. 
 Separate preview controls from access 
 Google supports page and text preview controls such as  nosnippet ,  max-snippet , and  data-nosnippet . Its  robots metadata documentation  explains their effects on snippets and AI inputs. Apply these with a specific goal, because they can also change ordinary Search presentation. 
 If the goal is complete removal from Google Search,  noindex has a different purpose . Google must be able to access the page to see that instruction. Blocking crawling in robots.txt can prevent it from reading the noindex rule. Have your implementer check the live response, not just a checkbox in the editor. 
  Google-Extended  is a robots.txt token for specified training and grounding uses in Gemini products, not a separate HTTP user-agent. Google says it does not determine Search inclusion or ranking. Keep an explicit record of your search-discovery policy and your model-training policy so a later security or hosting change does not confuse them. 
 Understand OpenAI’s three relevant agents 
 The names refer to different activities. The following distinctions come from  official OpenAI crawler documentation . 
    Agent  Documented purpose  Practical implication      OAI-SearchBot  Discovery for ChatGPT search  Opting out prevents appearance in search answers, though navigational links may remain    GPTBot  Crawling content that may be used for model training  Training preferences can differ from search preferences    ChatGPT-User  Certain visits initiated by a user  It is not the automatic search crawler, and robots.txt rules may not apply    
 OpenAI documents independent settings for search and training, and recommends allowing the published search-bot IP ranges when permitting search access. Do not assume that allowing one agent grants access to every activity. Review firewall rules alongside robots.txt; a hosting security layer can block requests before page content is reached. 
 Ask your host or developer for a narrow report: which relevant agent was allowed or denied, which public URL it requested, and when. A crawler visit establishes access at that time. It does not establish a citation, an endorsement, or a future stream of visitors. 
 Make the page worth visiting 
 Choose one customer question that requires a decision. For a booking business, that might be whether someone can reschedule, what information they need, and which deadline applies. Put the answer and conditions together. Add a helpful example, the exception that commonly causes confusion, and the next action. 
 For an advice article, separate what the source establishes from your recommendation. A useful format is: situation, options, tradeoff, recommended next step, and when to stop. Link the evidence beside the factual claim. Use the  AI-assisted content review workflow  if a model helped draft it. 
 Our editorial priority is distinctive help: a clearly labeled hypothetical decision example, an original checklist, or a documented test that you actually performed. Do not invent firsthand experience to make a page look authoritative. If you cannot add useful information, improve an existing page before creating another variation. 
 Measure visibility and business value separately 
 Google now documents a  Generative AI performance report  for AI Overviews and AI Mode impressions. It may be absent when there are too few impressions. The documented report groups impressions by dimensions including page, country, device, and date; it is not an AI conversion report. Discover has a separate report. 
 Use the  search-review worksheet  for a monthly review with three sections: 
   Visibility:  record the available AI impression totals and page breakdown, keeping dates and filters consistent. Record “unavailable” rather than pretending missing data is measured zero.   Visits:  inspect identifiable referral traffic in your analytics. Keep unattributed traffic separate. A referrer is a useful observation, not a complete inventory of every AI-assisted journey.   Outcomes:  record the meaningful action for that page, such as a completed inquiry or newsletter signup. Check that the form works before interpreting an absence of submissions.  
 Keep a change log next to the worksheet. If impressions rise after an update, describe the association and consider other changes before claiming causation. Repeating a prompt manually can be a qualitative spot check; one visible answer is not a representative market-share measurement. 
 Use a small first sprint 
 First, verify access and inclusion for five important pages. Second, fix one page whose answer is incomplete or hard to use. Third, add the appropriate internal links and check the page on a phone. Finally, save a measurement baseline and a dated change note. Keep the scope small enough that you can explain what changed and why. 
 Before paying for a visibility product, ask what it observes, which countries and prompts it samples, how often it checks, and whether its score predicts an outcome you care about. Use tools that help you make decisions. Do not substitute a proprietary score for evidence that readers can find, trust, and use your website.

title: Five free tools that help a small website make better decisions
searchText:
Five free tools that help a small website make better decisions What each tool actually tells you, where its evidence stops, and a simple way to turn reports into useful work. Tools  A small website does not need a large software stack to start improving. It needs a way to find problems, decide which ones matter, and confirm that a change helped. These five tools cover different questions; none provides a complete judgment of your business or your content. 
 This is a researched selection based on official documentation and public tool pages checked on October 29, 2026. We did not run comparative product tests or connect SaaSNoti accounts for this guide. The suggested routines and examples are our editorial recommendations. 
 Choose the question before opening a dashboard 
    Your question  Start here  Useful output      What does Google know about this page?  Search Console  Indexing evidence and search performance    Why might this page feel slow?  PageSpeed Insights  Performance diagnostics and available field data    Can Bing discover my important pages?  Bing Webmaster Tools  Bing indexing and crawl diagnostics    Is supported structured data readable?  Rich Results Test  Detected items, errors, and warnings    Is interest seasonal or changing?  Google Trends  Relative search-interest patterns    
 Use the  page-audit worksheet  to record the question, affected URL, evidence, proposed change, owner, and recheck date. A report earns its place when it changes a decision. Save screenshots or exports with the settings visible so a later comparison is meaningful. 
 1. Google Search Console: visibility and indexing 
  Search Console is free  and reports on your presence in Google Search. It includes query and page performance, indexing diagnostics, and alerts. Registration is not a condition of appearing in Google, but access to your own property’s reports lets you investigate rather than guess. 
 Start with a verified property and a shortlist of pages you actually want discovered.  URL Inspection  includes indexed information and a live test. An indexing request does not guarantee inclusion. 
  Our first task:  inspect the homepage, main service page, and one guide. Record their statuses before changing anything. If a guide is accessible but its indexed version is old, investigate the dates and crawl status. If Google chose a different canonical, understand that relationship before adding more pages. 
  Limit:  this is evidence about Google. A good indexing status does not establish that the article is accurate, that the contact form works, or that visitors will become customers. 
 2. PageSpeed Insights: performance questions 
  PageSpeed Insights  accepts a public page URL. Google lists it among its  free speed-testing tools . Its  documentation  distinguishes simulated lab diagnostics from real-user field data collected over a preceding 28-day period. Small or new pages may lack enough field data; an origin-level result may appear instead. 
  Our first task:  select a page that visitors use to decide or contact you. Record mobile and desktop results separately. Save the tested URL, date, and whether the field data describes the page or the whole origin. Pick one repeated, actionable issue that matches a visible user problem. 
 For example, if an enormous hero image appears to delay the main content, ask the implementer to reduce its delivery size while preserving a clear image. Then repeat the test under comparable conditions and use the page yourself. Treat this as a hypothesis to check, not a guaranteed diagnosis. 
  Limit:  a lab score is not the experience of every visitor. Missing field data is not a failure, and a better score does not prove improved sales. 
 3. Bing Webmaster Tools: a second search view 
 Microsoft describes  Bing Webmaster Tools as free . Its documented features include site verification, URL inspection, search performance, sitemap reporting, and technical scans. It also supports importing verified sites from Google Search Console. 
  Our first task:  add the site through  the official service , complete ownership verification, and inspect the same three pages you checked in Google. Keep a separate column for Bing’s observations. If one engine reports a fetch problem, investigate the exact URL and response rather than assuming that the other engine’s successful fetch settles it. 
 Use a technical scan as a list of candidate fixes. A duplicated description across several pages may deserve attention, but a working lead form usually deserves attention sooner than a cosmetic score. Assign priorities based on the reader’s task and the evidence. 
  Limit:  Bing’s observations do not replace Google’s or measure every AI search service. The number of findings is not a reliable measure of business risk. Review the specific findings. 
 4. Rich Results Test: inspect supported markup 
 Google’s public  Rich Results Test  provides URL and code inputs without a paid subscription. It checks structured data relevant to supported Google rich results. Google’s  policies  require accurate markup; passing does not guarantee a rich result. 
  Our first task:  test one representative article or product page after your template adds structured data. Read which item type was detected, then compare its name, author, price, or other relevant fields with what a visitor actually sees. Correct contradictory values at their source so future pages inherit the fix. 
 Do not invent reviews, ratings, or product offers to make a test look better. If the tool detects no supported item, first ask whether the page has a legitimate reason to use one. Not every page needs extra markup. 
  Limit:  passing a machine check does not establish editorial truth or guarantee a search feature. A warning and an error also deserve different investigation; read the explanation before making a site-wide change. 
 5. Google Trends: relative interest and timing 
 Google’s training describes  Trends Explore as free . The  data FAQ  explains that results use sampled searches normalized to a 0–100 scale. The numbers are relative interest, not monthly search volumes; low-volume terms can display zero. 
  Our first task:  compare two plausible topic ideas using the same country, time period, search type, and category. Record whether each selection is a search term or a topic. Examine a longer period for recurring seasonality before interpreting a short spike as an enduring opportunity. 
 Suppose a business is deciding when to publish a preparation guide for a seasonal service. Use the observed pattern to propose a publication window, then check actual customer questions and your ability to help. This is a planning example; we are not claiming measured demand for a particular service. 
  Limit:  relative interest does not tell you competition, purchase intent, profitability, or the exact number of people searching. Use the  article planning checklist  before turning a trend into a brief. 
 Turn the tools into a small routine 
   At launch:  verify search properties, inspect key pages, check the main page templates, and save a performance baseline.   After an important change:  revisit the tool that answers the original question. Confirm the changed page and the next action work on a phone.   Monthly:  review useful pages, new issues, and actual inquiries. Select one content improvement and one technical issue with clear evidence.  
 When a report is empty, write down the limitation. When two reports differ, compare what they measure before choosing a winner. These habits are more valuable than collecting screenshots of high scores. Keep the stack small enough that each report leads to an action you can explain.

title: Change Squarespace URLs without sending visitors to dead ends
searchText:
Change Squarespace URLs without sending visitors to dead ends Build a redirect map, choose relevant destinations, and test the result before and after a URL change. SEO basics 
 A redirect is a route from an old address to a new one. It is useful when a page moves, but it cannot repair an unrelated replacement page or guarantee that search traffic stays unchanged. The work begins before you edit a slug: decide which addresses genuinely need to change and what a visitor should find at each destination. 
 This guide gives you a small-site migration worksheet and an original test routine. The example URLs are fictional. We have not performed a traffic experiment on them, and the examples are not a promise that a particular redirect will preserve rankings. 
 First decide whether the URL needs to change 
 You can improve a weak headline, rewrite an opening, or update a service description without automatically renaming its address. In Squarespace, changing a page title does not require changing its slug. Blog post addresses include the blog collection slug, and a changed default post format applies to future posts rather than retroactively updating existing ones.  Check the URL slug controls.  
 Before changing anything, write a one-sentence reason: “We are merging two outdated checklists into a complete current guide,” or “This service has been renamed and the old URL causes customer confusion.” “The URL could contain one more keyword” is usually a weak reason for creating migration work on its own. 
 Separate a title change from a move in your task list. Give the URL work an owner and a rollback note. If the site has important inbound links or active advertising, include those destinations in the review rather than judging the change from the navigation menu alone. 
 Build a one-row-per-address map 
 Start with a spreadsheet containing the old full URL, proposed full URL, reason, action, responsible person, and test result. Collect addresses from your actual pages, analytics, search reports, campaign links, and important downloadable documents. A visual redesign can hide an old page without removing the links that still lead to it. 
    Old path  Proposed destination  Decision      /team-photos  /team-headshots  Permanent replacement with equivalent purpose    /blog/headshot-prep  /articles/headshot-preparation  Revised article covering the same preparation task    /winter-mini-sessions  No suitable replacement yet  Review; do not force it to the homepage    /contact  /contact  Keep; no redirect required    
 Add a relevance note in plain language: “A visitor following the old link still gets the staff-photo service they requested.” If that sentence feels dishonest, the destination is wrong. For a retired seasonal offer, you might keep a useful explanation or let a removed page return a proper not-found response, depending on the actual business situation. 
 Google warns against redirecting many old addresses to an irrelevant destination such as the homepage. A suitable consolidated replacement is different: it should actually contain the information the old pages offered.  Google's site-move guidance  covers mapping and relevance. 
 Choose permanent or temporary deliberately 
 Use a permanent redirect for a lasting move and a temporary redirect when you intend to restore the original address. Google treats permanent and temporary redirects differently as canonicalization signals; neither category is a guarantee about a page's future position.  Read Google's redirect documentation.  
 For a small permanent Squarespace move, the mapping syntax is  /old-path -> /new-path 301 . The old route must no longer resolve as an active page. Open Developer tools, then URL mappings; put more specific rules above broad rules. The panel works for domains connected to that Squarespace site, and it cannot redirect CDN image or file URLs.  Squarespace documents the format and restrictions.  
 For our fictional team-photography page, the entry would be  /team-photos -> /team-headshots 301 . Create and check the replacement first. Save the previous page text and settings before disabling or renaming the old route, so reversing an accidental change is possible. 
 Use individual rules for a short list of important pages. A broad collection rule may be convenient later, but it deserves its own test cases. Do not paste an example into your live settings without replacing the sample paths and checking for conflicts with existing rules. 
 Test the whole journey, not just the new page 
 Opening the new page proves only that the new page exists. It does not prove that an old newsletter link reaches it. Use this repeatable review for every mapped address: 
  Open a private browser window so you see the public experience.  Enter the complete old URL exactly as it appeared in the inventory.  Check the final address and read enough of the destination to confirm that it answers the old request.  Use your browser's Network panel with its log preserved to check the first document response and any subsequent redirects. Record the status and destination.  Open the final URL directly. Confirm it serves a working public page rather than another redirect, login, draft, or error.  Follow a relevant internal link and the page's main action. Verify that the move did not strand the customer elsewhere.  
 A successful response alone is not evidence of indexing or usefulness. Google can identify error-like content served with a success status as a soft 404.  Google's status-code reference  explains the distinction. A beautiful “page not found” message with a success response is not a successful migration. 
 In your worksheet, save a compact test note such as “Old URL returns 301; final URL returns 200; correct service and contact link checked.” If there are several hops, identify the intermediate rule and try to point the original route directly to the final destination. Keep the old-to-new map even after the first review passes. 
 Understand which host controls the old address 
 A redirect instruction has to reach the server handling the old URL. Adding a rule on your new Squarespace site cannot change a response from an unrelated GitHub Pages address.
