That follows from Squarespace's connected-domain restriction: the new platform does not receive that old request in the first place. 
 For a shareable development preview, the practical handoff is to keep the preview clearly labeled and link people to the final site when it launches. For an established production domain, plan the old-host behavior and domain connection together. A domain purchase, a DNS change, and a page redirect are separate actions; writing a mapping spreadsheet does not perform any of them. 
 Check the move after launch 
 Update your own links to use the final addresses, review the new sitemap, and watch for unexpected missing pages. Google recommends retaining migration redirects for at least a year where possible and notes that search visibility can fluctuate during a move.  Keep the migration guidance available  while monitoring. 
 Our suggested review rhythm is immediately after the change, the next working day, and weekly during the initial rollout. This is an operating checklist, not a guaranteed recovery timetable. Record the exact date of the move and distinguish broken routes from changes in demand, new content, or other changes made at the same time. 
 If inquiries disappear, verify the contact journey before rewriting every title. If a specific old link fails, repair that mapping. The worksheet should make the next action obvious: one address, one intended destination, and a test you can repeat.

title: Fix heavy Squarespace pages without chasing a perfect speed score
searchText:
Fix heavy Squarespace pages without chasing a perfect speed score An image inventory, a repeatable mobile test, and a decision table for the performance problems you can actually change. Tools 
 A slow page is easier to improve when you can name the thing making it slow. “Squarespace is slow” and “the score is orange” are not useful diagnoses. A huge hero image, several video embeds, a busy third-party widget, and a shifting booking form are different problems with different fixes. 
 Use this original audit routine on one important page at a time. It focuses on changes a small-site owner can inspect and reverse. It is not a benchmark of Squarespace, and the worked example below is invented to demonstrate the decision process rather than report measured results. 
 Pick a page and a real visitor task 
 Choose a page that matters to your business: the service page someone uses before requesting a quote, a guide people actually read, or the booking page itself. Write down the task you will test, such as “Read the offer, open the pricing detail, and start an inquiry.” 
 Test while logged out. Open the page on a phone, scroll through it, use its menu, and try the primary action. Note what you experience in ordinary language: “The main image appears late,” “The button moves as I tap,” or “The form ignores the first tap.” Save those observations before changing the design. 
 Keep the baseline simple: page URL, test date, device, network, visible problem, and report link. If someone else repeats your audit, they should know which page and task you meant. Do not compare a desktop homepage test with a mobile article test and call the difference an improvement. 
 Read the report in two parts 
 PageSpeed Insights combines a simulated Lighthouse test with historical real-user data when enough data is available. Its field data uses a trailing 28-day period; it may show origin-level data or none at all for a small site. Missing field data is not a failed performance test.  Google explains the report's data sources.  
 Record whether you are looking at this URL or the whole origin. Then separate the user metric from the diagnostic suggestion. The current Core Web Vitals are LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness, and CLS for visual stability. The good thresholds are at most 2.5 seconds, 200 milliseconds, and 0.1 respectively, evaluated at the 75th percentile.  web.dev explains the thresholds.  
 You do not need to memorize every acronym to make a first improvement. Match the report to a visible symptom and to something you can control. If a suggestion concerns the platform's own core scripts, keep it in a separate list from your oversized uploads and optional widgets. Escalate platform-level issues with the page URL and evidence instead of installing another optimization script at random. 
 Make an image inventory before compressing everything 
 List each important image's role, original filename, dimensions, upload size, where it appears, and whether small text must remain readable. Add a keep, replace, or remove decision. A screenshot demonstrating a setting may be essential; three decorative versions of the same idea may not be. 
 Squarespace currently accepts JPG, GIF, PNG, and static WebP uploads, with a 20 MB limit, and recommends 500 KB or less for loading speed. It normally serves uploaded images as WebP and creates responsive variants. Its general width recommendation is 2500 pixels for most images; that is a platform guideline, not a reason to enlarge a tiny original.  Check the current image requirements.  
    Image role  Practical review  Success check      Large photograph  Crop to the intended composition and export a smaller copy  Looks clean at its real display size    Screenshot with instructions  Crop to the relevant control; keep the labels readable  A phone reader can follow the instruction    Logo or transparent artwork  Use a supported format that preserves the required edges and transparency  No blurred outline or unwanted background    Repeated decorative image  Ask whether it adds information on this page  The page still feels complete if removed    
 Keep the original outside the website editor. Change one export variable at a time and use descriptive working filenames, such as “team-session-hero-cropped.” Do not overwrite the only high-resolution copy. Compare the result at the actual on-page size instead of zooming into it far beyond how visitors will see it. 
 Reduce the total page load 
 Several individually reasonable images can still make a heavy page. Squarespace suggests keeping pages at 5 MB or less where possible and provides a Network-panel method for identifying large resources. It also recommends limiting video-heavy pages and using blog excerpts instead of full posts on a slow index.  See its page-size guide.  
 Our preferred first pass is an editorial one. Remove a duplicate image before reducing the readability of a necessary diagram. Replace a nonessential embedded video with a clear link if the visitor can complete the task without playing it. Keep an important booking tool, but investigate whether it must load on every page. 
 Make a short ownership list for third-party additions: name, purpose, pages where needed, and person who can disable it. A widget installed for an old campaign is easy to forget. Test removal in a reversible copy or controlled change, and verify that analytics, contact forms, and booking still work afterward. 
 Keep the images useful and accessible 
 Speed improvements should not remove the information an image exists to communicate. Put essential instructions in text as well as a screenshot. For a service photo, describe what matters in context rather than filling the description with repeated location keywords. 
 Squarespace image blocks have a dedicated alt-text field. The platform's current AI SEO report does not scan images in collection items, so a completed report is not evidence that every blog illustration has been reviewed.  Read the alt-text instructions and scope.  
 A useful manual check is to read the surrounding paragraph without the image. If a reader loses a required step, add that step to the text. Then ask whether the image description communicates the remaining relevant visual information. A decorative flourish and an instructional screenshot have different jobs; do not automatically give both the article title as alt text. 
 Work through a fictional audit 
 Imagine a service page with a large office photograph, eight project images, two video embeds, and a scheduling widget. The owner observes that the first image appears late and the booking area jumps while loading. No measurements in this example are real. 
   Inventory:  keep the useful project examples, identify repeated images, and note the scheduling tool's owner.   First change:  export a smaller hero image and compare its crop on phone and desktop. Retest the same task.   Second change:  move one optional video to a related detail page and use a descriptive link. Retest again.   Separate issue:  examine the scheduling area for reserved space or an alternative layout. A lighter photograph does not necessarily fix its movement.   Record:  note what changed, whether the visible problem improved, and whether the inquiry route still works.  
 The point is to connect a symptom to a change you can evaluate. Keep a useful image if removing it makes the service harder to understand. Undo a cosmetic speed win if it breaks the next step. Continue with the  blog publishing checklist  when the page is usable and ready for its content review. 
 Decide when to stop this pass 
 Finish when the essential task works, the obvious excess is removed, and the remaining problems have a clear owner. Save the before-and-after report links and a short change log. Revisit field data later rather than expecting a 28-day history to instantly reflect today's edit. 
 A perfect laboratory score is not the business outcome. A reader who can see the information, use the controls, and complete the intended action gives you a much more useful target.
